Which rescue for the word 'heap' seems most sensible to you?
How often does the sorites paradox cross your mind when you use words like 'tall' or 'rich'?
options: It has never crossed your mind
It crosses your mind in arguments about definitions
It comes up for you in daily speech

text: If a grain-by-grain argument proves there are no heaps, would you rather reject logic or reject heaps?
A car goes 1 km/h faster each second. When is it 'fast'?
Is 'borderline heap' a real category, not just our ignorance?
You add one cent to a poor person's savings each day. When is it true that they are no longer poor?
options: On an exact cent, knowable in principle
On an exact cent, knowable to no one
In a stretch of days where both labels fit

text: A novel gains one page at a time. When does it become a long novel?
Does the puzzle bother you more for grains of sand or for the moment a person dies?
Which do you think is the most honest answer to 'is 180 cm tall?'
How would you grade the claim that 'heap' has a precise boundary we just can't see?
Is there a first moment at which a growing child becomes 'a teenager in spirit', or only a blur?
Two strangers chat a little more each week. When are they friends?
Would it change your answer if the grains were removed by a machine you couldn't see?
Which describes how you'd describe a man with a thin crown and full sides?
Do you think 'heap' means something different each time you use it, depending on context?
Where do you think the flaw lies in 'one grain never makes a difference'?
Cool the water by 0.1 degree at a time. How would you describe the point it stops being warm?
options: An exact temperature, unknown to us
No point: "warm" is not a fact about water

text: Would you accept that a statement can be half true, like 'this pile is a heap' being 0.5 true?
Add one appointment at a time. When is a day 'busy'?
Is 'late' for a meeting a sharp line at the scheduled minute?
Add 10 cents at a time to a $2 coffee. When is it an expensive coffee?
options: At an exact price for everyone
At a price that differs by city
Never a fact, only an opinion

text: A lineage changes one generation at a time. When does a new species appear?
Are vague words like 'heap' a flaw in language that a better language would fix?
Sorites for a crowd at a gig: how many people must be in a small bar before you'd call it crowded?
Add one employee at a time. Which answer seems right to you?
Does the fact that people agree on clear heaps and clear non-heaps show the word works fine?
The opaque box holds $1,000,000 if a predictor foresaw you taking only it; the clear box holds $1,000. Which do you take?
If a real predictor with a 95% record set up the boxes for you tomorrow, which would you take?
You two-box and the opaque box turns out empty. What is your verdict on your own choice?
options: It was right: the money was never there
You now doubt it was right
It was a mistake: one-boxers got rich

text: Newcomb's problem with a predictor who is your oldest friend and knows you well: which do you take?
If the clear box held $900,000 instead of $1,000, would you switch to taking both?
Which argument pulls on you hardest?
If twenty friends each argued the other side, how firmly would you keep your answer?
Does knowing the predictor is a brain scanner rather than a psychic change your choice?
You get $1 million if at midnight you intend to drink a harmless but nasty toxin tomorrow. What happens?
Once paid at midnight, should you still drink the toxin the next day?
A driver saves you from the desert if you promise $100 on arrival. Once in town, how binding is that promise?
options: Not binding: the danger is over
Binding even if it cost far more

text: Death, who predicts your moves, says he'll meet you tomorrow. Where do you go?
A stranger says pay $10 or he'll use magic powers to harm a billion people. Is refusing the rational call?
How small would the chance of the stranger's story need to be before you'd ignore any promised reward?
options: No chance is small enough if the reward is huge enough

text: St. Petersburg game: a coin is flipped until heads; the pot doubles each tails. Most you'd pay to play once?
St. Petersburg paradox: does the game's infinite expected payout make it worth paying $1,000 to play once?
First, $1 million for sure or a 10% shot at $5 million, 89% at $1 million, 1% at nothing. Which?
11% at $1 million, or 10% at $5 million. Which do you pick?
If picking the sure million and then the 10% shot breaks a rule of rational choice, is that a flaw in you or in the rule?
Urn A has 50 red and 50 black balls; urn B's mix is unknown. Win $100 on red. Which urn?
How much extra would you pay to draw from the urn with the known mix?
One holds twice the other. You open yours and see $100. Would you switch?
Which diagnosis seems right to you?
Woken, not knowing if it's Monday or Tuesday, with a coin toss deciding one or two wakings. Your credence that the coin landed heads?
options: Between a third and a half

text: Which camp are you in?
He can't tell the first exit from the second. Should he plan as if he were at the first exit?
A gene causes both a harmless cigarette craving and cancer. Should you smoke if you crave it?
Prisoner's dilemma with a perfect copy of yourself: cooperate or defect?
The prisoner's dilemma, one round with a stranger: how likely are you to cooperate?
Would you cooperate if the stranger could see your choice before making theirs?
Iterated prisoner's dilemma over 50 rounds with the same player: what is your opening move?
A donkey dies of hunger between two identical hay bales. Could a truly rational agent get stuck like that?
Faced with two identical offers, what would you do?
If you were the donkey between two equal bales, what would break the tie for you?
Two drivers race toward each other; the first to swerve loses face. What is your strategy?
Is throwing your steering wheel out the window a clever move?
You're offered $20 out of $100, take it or both get nothing. What do you do?
What is the lowest share of $100 you would accept?
You get $100 to split with a stranger who can't respond. How much do you give?
Two travelers each name a price between $2 and $100 for identical lost luggage; the lower claim wins a bonus. Would you claim $100?
Hunting a stag needs both partners; a rabbit you can catch alone. Which do you go for?
How much would you trust a stranger to hold out for the stag with you?
options: You wouldn't trust them at all
You'd trust them if they promised
You'd trust them even after a past lapse

text: Is it irrational to spend an hour voting when one ballot will almost never change the result?
Both boxes are clear and you can see the $1,000,000. Which do you take?
A tiny chance of an enormous reward for a small cost. How persuasive is that shape of argument?
Is it rational to buy a lottery ticket you are sure will lose?
After the host opens a goat door, which feels right before you think?
Did the Monty Hall puzzle's answer strike you as obviously wrong when you first met it, as it does most people?
A friend offers either a sealed envelope or a known $50. You're told most people who took the envelope were happy. Which?
Is a choice between one option and nothing a real choice?
Do you think your answer reveals whether you believe in free will?
The predictor filled the boxes a year ago. Which do you take?
Which test would you trust most to show you're awake right now?
How seriously do you take the idea that this moment could be a dream?
options: Not at all a live option
A real possibility you can't rule out

text: If a dream were perfectly vivid and consistent, would anything still separate it from waking life?
A scientist feeds your brain a perfect simulated world. Which do you find most convincing?
Suppose you learned you were envatted. What would your past experiences be worth to you?
If you were envatted, would your thought 'I have hands' be false?
A demon deceives you about everything it can. What survives the doubt, in your view?
Can a demon fool you about the fact that you are being fooled?
You check a stopped clock that happens to show the right time. Do you know the time?
Should luck ever disqualify a true belief from being knowledge?
Should the fake barns nearby, which you never looked at, decide whether you know the real one?
What do they do to the idea that knowledge is justified true belief?
Fed every morning for a year, then killed. What lesson does the puzzle teach you?
Is it reasonable to expect the sun to rise tomorrow without a proof that it will?
How comfortable are you relying on 'it has always happened' in daily life?
'grue' means green before 2030, blue after. Why prefer 'green' for predicting emeralds?
If a society had grown up using 'grue', would their predictions be just as rational as ours?
A white sneaker confirms 'all non-black things are non-ravens'. Does it support 'all ravens are black'?
How troubling is it that your laundry could count as evidence about ravens?
options: A crisis for how evidence works

text: A teacher says a surprise test comes next week. The students reason it can't happen. What do you say?
If the test lands on Wednesday, were the students actually surprised?
Which sentence strikes you as the strangest thing a person could say?
Can a sentence be true and yet absurd for anyone to assert?
How do you think we search for something we don't yet know?
An author believes each claim in her book but also that the book contains an error. How rational is she?
Can it be rational to believe your ticket will lose but still keep it?
Which rule do you find most appealing?
The world, with all its memories, began five minutes ago. How would you rate the idea?
options: A real challenge to what you know

text: If everything began five minutes ago with fake memories, would you have any evidence against it?
Prisoners see only shadows on a wall. Which modern thing do you think best fits the cave?
Would a freed prisoner who returned to describe the sun be believed?
Melt a candle, and every sensed quality changes. What is your verdict on whether it's the same wax?
A person born blind who knows shapes by touch gains sight. Would they recognize a cube by sight at once?
Do sight and touch share one idea of 'round'?
What is your best reason to think other people have inner lives?
How certain are you that a stranger on the bus has feelings like yours?
Is it more likely that a lone brain with false memories popped into existence than that the universe is as it seems?
Which option do you find most likely?
How would learning we live in a simulation change how you rate the reality of your life?
options: Unchanged: it's still real to you

text: If we are simulated, would the people you love still be real in every way that matters?
If every truth could be known, all truths would be known. What gives, in your view?
Do you think there are truths no one could ever know?
Sam knows Ana, but can't say who the hooded man is, and the hooded man is Ana. Does Sam know the hooded man?
How convincing is 'I know X, I don't know the masked man, so the masked man isn't X'?
If you know something, you should ignore all future evidence against it. What's wrong?
Should someone who truly knows a fact refuse to read a book arguing the opposite?
If a definition is correct it says nothing new, and if new, not correct. Which do you believe?
The Mary's room puzzle as a knowledge test: after seeing red for the first time, how much new knowledge does Mary gain?
options: A new way of knowing an old fact
A whole new kind of fact

text: Could Mary have predicted exactly what red would look like from her books?
Nozick's experience of the tree in the forest: if a tree falls and no one hears it, does it make a sound?
Is it a real puzzle rather than just a quarrel about the word 'sound'?
Which belief would you find hardest to doubt even for a moment?
What effect do they have on what you actually believe day to day?
options: They shape how you hold every belief

text: If you were offered a pill to find out whether you're envatted, would you take it?
Hypothetically, if a scientist offered proof you were in a simulation, would you want to see it?
Which feature of waking life do you think no dream could fake?
A man with a rulebook passes notes in fluent Chinese without knowing a word. Who, if anyone, understands Chinese?
How well does the puzzle show that following rules is not the same as understanding?
If the man memorized the whole rulebook and did it in his head, would he then understand Chinese?
Put the room inside a robot that sees and moves. Would it understand then?
How many hours of flawless conversation would it take to convince you the room understands?
A color scientist raised in black and white sees a red apple for the first time. What does she gain?
Would Mary be surprised when she first saw red?
How strong is the puzzle as a case that the mind is more than physical?
A being physically identical to you but with no inner experience. Is such a being possible?
If you learned a close friend was a perfect philosophical zombie, would you treat them any differently?
How easily can you imagine a perfect copy of a person with nothing going on inside?
Suppose your red looks like my green, but we both call ripe tomatoes red. What follows?
Could two people have swapped color experiences and never discover it?
A bat navigates by echolocation. Can a human ever know what it's like to be a bat?
What Is It Like to Be a Bat?: how much do you think science could ever tell us about the bat's inner experience?
Every person in China simulates one neuron by radio. Would China as a whole have experiences?
If the nation-wide system reported pain, should anyone take the report seriously?
Walk inside a thinking machine enlarged to the size of a mill. What would you see that explains thought?
How troubling is the point that no single gear or lever looks like a thought?
options: Not troubling: that's how systems work

text: Everyone has a box only they can see into, holding a 'beetle'. What does 'beetle' refer to?
Could the word 'pain' work fine even if each person's pain felt completely different?
Lightning strikes a swamp and creates an exact molecular copy of a man who just died. Does Swampman have thoughts?
When Swampman says 'my wife', is he referring to the dead man's wife?
On a twin planet, 'water' names a liquid with a different chemistry that looks and acts the same. Do the twins mean the same by 'water'?
How convinced are you that meaning depends on the world and not just on what's in the head?
'If a lion could talk, we could not understand him.' Your verdict?
A speaker points at a rabbit and says 'gavagai'. What does the word mean?
Could two translators give different but equally correct translations of the same language?
What fixes that by '+' you have always meant addition and not some odd rule?
How troubling is the idea that past use doesn't settle what a word means?
'the morning star' and 'the evening star' both name Venus. Is 'the morning star is the evening star' news?
Could someone rationally believe that the morning star is bright but the evening star is not?
Could someone invent a word for a sensation only they could ever check?
What's your gut reaction to physicalists saying Mary learns nothing new?
The hard problem of consciousness as a puzzle: why should brain processes feel like anything at all?
If zombies are conceivable, does that show consciousness is something extra beyond the physical?
Neurons are swapped for chips one by one while you watch colors. What happens to your experience?
After the cut, how many minds are in the skull?
options: One or two, by the task

text: Does the idea show that color experiences can't be fully described in words?
Which reply do you find strongest?
Does the puzzle make you less confident that science can explain everything?
What if Mary had been shown a red apple in a dream before leaving the room?
How strongly does the puzzle suggest that inner feelings can't be shared in words?
Which do you find closer to the man in the room?
Is passing every conversation test enough to count as understanding, whatever is inside?
Mary leaves, sees red, then forgets what it looked like but keeps the facts. What has she lost?
How easily could you tell a zombie from a person in a week of chatting?
Should Swampman be allowed to keep the dead man's job and house?
Animals on a far planet look exactly like tigers but are reptiles. Are they tigers?
You design a society not knowing if you'll be born rich or poor. Which rule do you pick?
How much average income would you give up to raise the floor for the worst-off?
Would a person behind the veil gamble on being born into the top 1%?
A whole city's happiness depends on one child's misery. What would you do?
Is walking away from Omelas enough, or does it just keep your own hands clean?
A being gets vastly more joy from each resource than anyone else. How much should it get?
Which world is better?
How repugnant does it really seem to you?
options: So repugnant it refutes the theory

text: Can a choice harm future people if without it they would never have existed?
Saving a child from a pond would ruin your $300 shoes. What should you do?
If saving the drowning child is required, is donating $300 to save a distant child equally required?
How strong is the move from the pond to distant strangers?
A captain will spare nineteen prisoners if Jim shoots one. What should Jim do?
If Jim refuses and all twenty die, is he partly responsible?
A ring makes you invisible at will. What would most people do with it?
If you found the ring on a walk, would you keep it?
How many people do you think would stay fully honest with it?
You find a fence across a road with no obvious purpose. What should you do?
Is 'find out why it's there first' good advice for old rules too?
A shared pasture is overgrazed because each herder adds one more cow. Best fix?
What do you expect when strangers share a free fishing lake with no rules?
options: It is emptied within a season
It declines until someone sets rules
It holds up with some grumbling
It is shared well for years

text: People who chase happiness directly find less of it. Your view?
Can someone who constantly asks 'am I happy?' ever be fully happy?
Why do people cry over characters they know don't exist?
How strange is it that people enjoy watching sad plays?
Two drivers text at the wheel; one hits a child, the other gets home safely. How should they be blamed?
Is it fair that outcomes you couldn't control change how much you are blamed?
A street party is funded by donations, but everyone enjoys it. What happens without a rule?
A killer asks where your friend is hiding. Must you tell the truth?
How wrong is lying to the killer, in your view?
Which do you think future generations will judge us most harshly for?
The paradox of tolerance, in a club setting: should a book club that welcomes every view expel a member who bullies others out?
Two equally needy people, one kidney. How should it be decided?
A 14-year-old waits until 25 to have a child, so a different child is born. How much better is waiting?
A technician is getting painful shocks; saving him means interrupting a World Cup broadcast for millions. What should be done?
Can enough small pleasures ever outweigh one person's severe pain?
Threatening to retaliate prevents attack, but carrying it out would be wrong. What follows?
How close is our world to Omelas, in your view?
Would you choose the same rules if you knew you'd be born healthy?
The last human alive cuts down the last tree. Did he do anything wrong?
How wrong would it be for him to destroy the last forest before he dies?
A wise ruler would run things better than voters. What's your verdict?
Would it change your answer if the child did not know they were suffering?
The liar paradox on a sticky note: the note says 'The sentence on this note is false.' Which label fits the note best?
How much does it bother you?
options: Not a bit: it's a word trick

text: Does 'this sentence is not true' defeat the answer that the liar sentence is neither true nor false?
Epimenides the Cretan says 'All Cretans are liars.' What follows?
One side says 'the other side is true', the other says 'the other side is false'. Which side is true?
A village barber shaves all and only those who don't shave themselves. How do you rate the puzzle?
Is the simple answer 'there can't be such a barber' fully satisfying?
'heterological' means a word that doesn't describe itself. Is 'heterological' heterological?
'the smallest number not nameable in under eleven words' is named in ten. What went wrong?
'If this sentence is true, then dragons exist' seems to prove dragons exist. How bothered are you?
Can an endless list of sentences, each saying all later ones are false, create a paradox without any sentence referring to itself?
A crocodile promises to return a child if the parent correctly predicts what it will do. The parent says 'You won't return it.' What should the crocodile do?
A student owes his fee once he wins his first case, then is sued for the fee. Who should win?
Should the judge rule for the student now, knowing the teacher can sue again and win?
His nose grows only when he lies, and he announces that it is growing right now. Your verdict on the nose?
How good an illustration of the liar paradox is it?
Can a being that can do anything make a stone it cannot lift?
Does it show that 'can do anything' is an incoherent idea?
'there will be a sea battle tomorrow' is either true or false today. Does that make tomorrow fixed?
How convincing is 'what will happen is already true, so you can't change it'?
If it's already true that you'll order soup tomorrow, are you still free to order salad?
A catalog lists all catalogs that don't list themselves. Should it list itself?
How much should ordinary people care that set theory once broke over it?
Can a sentence say 'no one knows this sentence is true' and be known?
A time traveler gives Shakespeare his own plays, which Shakespeare publishes. Who wrote them?
How troubling is information with no origin?
options: Proof that such time travel is impossible

text: A time traveler tries to stop their own grandparents from meeting. What happens?
Do you think it proves backward time travel is impossible?
A post reads 'Every post on this site is false.' What is the post?
A says 'B is true', B says 'A is false'. Is there any consistent way to assign truth?
A friend says 'I'll tell you one lie today, and you won't spot it.' Can the promise be kept?
Where do they matter outside philosophy classes?
Listing every number describable in English leads to a number described but not listed. Your verdict?
Would you accept that some sentences are both true and false?
The paradox of the preface in logic class: a student is sure each answer is right and sure one is wrong. What should they do?
How good is it as an argument that 'all-powerful' is incoherent?
If Allen goes out, Brown must go with him; someone must mind the shop. Which puzzle-solving style do you trust?
Does it show that 'if...then' is more slippery than it looks?
Which self-reference paradox do you find most gripping?
A witness swears 'Everything I say today is false.' How should a judge treat the testimony?
options: Treat it as a puzzle to be ruled on

text: Is a paradox with no solution a sign that the world itself is contradictory?
The paradox of the heap vs the liar: which do you think will be resolved first?
How quickly did (or would) you spot the problem when you first hear it?
Is the crocodile obliged to keep the child once the parent's prediction makes the promise impossible?
When a chain of obvious steps leads to an absurd conclusion, what do you usually suspect?
To cross a room you must first cross half, then half the rest, forever. What's your gut reaction?
At every instant a flying arrow occupies one spot, so it never moves. How strong is the argument?
Does the math of infinite series fully settle Zeno's paradox for you?
One grain falls silently, yet a bushel falls with a roar. Where does the sound come from?
What is their status today, in your view?
Every room is full, yet a new guest is fit in by shifting everyone up one room. Your reaction?
Does the story convince you that an actual infinite collection could never exist in the real world?
Switched on at 1 minute, off at half a minute more, on at a quarter more, and so on. At the 2-minute mark, is it on or off?
How troubling is the lack of an answer about the final state?
options: A reason to reject infinite tasks

text: Infinitely many reapers each strike if you're still alive at earlier and earlier moments. What kills you?
Tristram Shandy takes a year to write each day of his life. If he lived forever, would every day eventually be written up?
Every whole number has a square, yet squares seem rarer. Are there as many squares as numbers?
The Ross–Littlewood vase: at each step 10 balls go in and 1 comes out, faster and faster. What does your gut say is in the vase at noon?
Two joined circles roll the same distance though one is smaller. How puzzling is it to you?
The statue and the lump of clay: a sculptor shapes clay into a statue. How many objects are on the plinth?
If the statue is squashed, has something been destroyed even though no clay was lost?
Is a hole in a slice of cheese a real thing?
How confident are you that holes exist in their own right?
Cut off Tibbles's tail, and 'Tibbles minus tail' and Tibbles now occupy the same place. How many cats are there?
Theon is Dion minus his left foot. Dion's foot is amputated. Who survives?
A cloud has no sharp edge. Is there exactly one cloud in the sky?
Two identical iron spheres in otherwise empty space. Are they two things?
How convincing is the case that two things can share every property?
After every drop of water has flowed past, what's left of the river you stepped in yesterday?
options: Nothing: it is a new river

text: Is a person the same person after every cell has been replaced, in the same sense a river is the same river?
Is time's passing real, or just how things seem?
The present-moment puzzle: how long is 'now'?
Is the future less real than the past?
If every moment is equally real, why does this one feel special?
A man walks toward a mile marker; infinitely many gods each raise a barrier if he reaches their point. What stops him?
What do they do to your trust in everyday reasoning?
If every cause needs a cause, can there be an infinite chain with no first cause?
Which reply would you give a friend in one breath?
Is motion a real feature of the world, beyond an object being in different places at different times?
The paradox of the growing heap in time: a stone wall ages one second at a time. When does it become an ancient wall?
After a flood reshapes a river's course, what's your verdict on whether it's the same river?
The ship is renamed but not repaired. Is it a different ship?
Could a person meet their younger self without any contradiction?
A time traveler steps on a butterfly in 65 million BC. What is your best guess about the result?
How strong a case do they make that backward time travel is impossible?
Does it bother you that your answer could make there be two cats where you see one?
Halfway through carving, is there a statue yet?
What is your reaction to the idea that 'infinity plus one' is still infinity?
A staircase goes down forever with no bottom step. Could it exist?
Two rows of runners pass each other twice as fast as they pass a still row. Does this show time comes in smallest units?
Asking for money is legal and revealing a secret is legal, yet combining them is a crime. Your verdict?
How puzzling is it that two permitted acts become forbidden together?
'if you murder, you ought to do it gently' seems to imply you ought to murder. Where's the flaw?
Does 'you ought to help the robbery victim' imply there ought to be a robbery victim?
If giving a kidney to a stranger is good, why isn't it required?
Forgiving only what is forgivable seems empty. What does real forgiveness cover?
If a sentence is just, is showing mercy an injustice?
Can facts about how things are ever prove how things ought to be?
If 'good' meant 'pleasant', asking 'is pleasure good?' would be pointless. How convincing is that?
Is an act right because a wise judge approves it, or does the judge approve because it is right?
Wanting to stop wanting things is itself a want. Can you escape it?
Can a club rule that says 'this rule can never be changed' be changed by a vote?
A truly free gift creates a debt of gratitude. Can a gift ever be free?
How much of an obligation does a surprise gift of $50 create?
Three friends rank pizza, tacos and sushi so every option loses to another by majority. What should they eat?
Does it show that 'what the group wants' may not exist?
Both players promise to cooperate, but promises aren't enforced. What do you do?
Trusting a stranger can make them more trustworthy. What role should that play in the puzzle?
The paradox of the heap of sins: no single white lie makes someone a liar. Can a person become a liar by accumulation?
If we think past moral views were wrong, we should expect ours are too. What follows?
Do you expect people in 200 years to be shocked by something you see as normal?
Would a perfectly moral person be someone you'd want as a friend?
How appealing is a life devoted entirely to doing the most good?
If you could save a life for $5,000, should you give until you're as poor as those you help?
Is a moral theory refuted if it asks too much of ordinary people?
A mayor can prevent a riot only by lying to the press. Should the mayor lie?
How should the mayor feel after doing the necessary wrong?
The paradox of the expected good deed: helping when you expect praise feels less virtuous. Does the motive spoil the act?
If someone is content in chains, has their freedom been harmed?
A disaster is caused by a thousand people each doing a tiny part. Who is to blame?
How much blame goes to one of 1,000 people who each added a drop of pollution?
Getting even often makes things worse, yet feels just. Which reaction fits you?
Is it odd that punishing a wrongdoer doesn't undo the wrong but still feels fitting?
The paradox of the heap of duties: each extra favor asked of a kind neighbor is small. At what point may they refuse?
Someone reads a stranger's diary and never tells anyone. Was anyone wronged?
How should a wrong that no one ever discovers count?
options: As much as a discovered wrong

text: Is breaking a deathbed promise wrong if no living person knows?
Someone's reputation is smeared after they die. Were they harmed?
A promise to someone now dead versus one to the living. How does breaking the first compare?
Japan's Ise Shrine is rebuilt from new timber every 20 years. Applying the Ship of Theseus puzzle, how old is the shrine?
A classic car is rebuilt around nothing but its original ID plate. Is it the original car?
A kintsugi bowl is broken and mended with gold five times. In Ship of Theseus terms, how much of the original bowl is left?
The tower was rebuilt in 1950 on the old base with the old lamp. Which is the 1820 lighthouse?
If a Lego castle is taken apart and rebuilt with the same bricks, is it the same castle?
Two identical sailboats exchange every part one at a time. Afterward, which boat is which?
A grandfather's watch has kept only its case after decades of repairs. How would you describe it?
options: A new watch in an old case

text: If the discarded planks were burned, would the repaired ship's claim to be the original become stronger?
A carousel's 40 horses are replaced one per year. Ship of Theseus-style, when does it stop being the original carousel?
A play has run for 40 years with no original cast, set or costumes. Is it the same production?
A blade has been reforged, rehilted and resheathed over 300 years. How honest is calling it 'the king's sword'?
Is a family chili recipe changed one ingredient per generation still the same recipe?
New deck, new trucks, same wheels. What would a skater call it?
A pub keeps its name and sign but moves across the street. Same pub?
Does the answer change if the replacement planks were taken from a sister ship?
